paras: The killing of Charles Davis took place near Denmark, South Carolina, on August 27, 1910, when Davis, a Black man wanted for the killing of Lucy Dwight, was shot as he fled an arranged arrest by Magistrate S. G. Ray. He died of his wounds the next morning, and a coroner's jury in Orangeburg heard uncertain testimony on whether the dead man was in fact Davis. Local white papers in Orangeburg and Bamberg welcomed the shooting and praised the magistrate.

On the morning of August 15, Lucy Dwight was shot dead while working in a field near Bowman, in Orangeburg county. The Orangeburg Times and Democrat named Charlie Davis, a man who had recently come from Florida, as the gunman and called Dwight his former wife, while a Columbia State report reprinted in Bamberg called the accused "Charles Dwight" and said no motive was known. Bloodhounds from Dorchester county followed a trail toward Rowesville but gave it up.

On August 24 Governor M. F. Ansel offered a reward of $100 for Davis, who was believed to have escaped to Florida. The proclamation described him as "a very black negro, about 35 years old," six feet tall and a saw mill hand.

According to a Denmark dispatch of August 27, Magistrate Ray had found Davis working on the plantation of Col. S. G. Mayfield near Denmark several days earlier and arranged to take him when he came to the plantation residence for a settlement. When Davis saw the officer he ran for the woods and was shot in the back, but he was followed and captured. A Denmark doctor, Matthews, examined him at his drug store and pronounced the wound fatal, and Davis would make no statement.

Sheriff Salley of Orangeburg, who had warned the magistrate that Davis was dangerous, came to Denmark that afternoon. The Orangeburg dispatch said Davis was brought by train to the county jail that night and died there at 8:30 the next morning, while the Times and Democrat said the sheriff could not move him and that he died early Sunday.

A coroner's jury under foreman J. C. Kennerly viewed the body on August 28, and Dr. T. C. Doyle testified that death came from two gunshot wounds, one in the stomach and one in the left breast. Sheriff Salley told the jury that the arrest had been made under the Governor's proclamation and that he knew none of the circumstances of the shooting. The dead man was said to have used the name Mitchell, and because the first identification testimony did not satisfy the jury, it adjourned to hear others who knew Davis. Several Bowman men, including L. J. Smith, went to Orangeburg to identify the body, but no verdict of the inquest appears in the coverage.

Coverage came only from white South Carolina weeklies near the scene, and no Black newspaper in the collection reported the case. The Denmark dispatch ran in the Orangeburg Times and Democrat on August 30, in the Sumter Watchman and Southron on August 31 under "NEGRO FUGITIVE FATALLY SHOT," and in the Bamberg Herald on September 1. Each paper treated Davis's guilt as settled, and the Times and Democrat ended its version by saying that when he was shot "he met his just death."

The Bamberg Herald went further, writing that the capture would have "a wholesome effect upon the dark corners" and praising Ray in its local column: "Pity we did not have more officers like him." The same paper's Orangeburg dispatch was more cautious, calling Davis the "alleged slayer," reporting the doubt over identity and describing the body as "a typical African." A Bowman correspondent reported "much satisfaction" in that town at news of the capture.

The dispatch described a single shot in the back passing through the left shoulder and lungs, but the physician at the inquest found two wounds, in the stomach and left breast. The Bamberg Herald's local column named Ray as the man who fired, while its Orangeburg dispatch said Davis was taken by Ray's constable and a posse. The proclamation gave Davis's age as about 35, while the inquest report put the dead man at 50 to 60.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Davis
bases: A magistrate (or, in one account, his constable and a posse) shot a Black man wanted on a governor's reward proclamation as he fled an arranged arrest, and he died of the wounds (A5, A7, A9, A10).

The Denmark dispatch (A5, A7, A8), a separate Orangeburg dispatch on the death and inquest (A9), the Bowman correspondent (A6) and the Bamberg Herald's own local item (A10) agree that Davis was shot while being arrested near Denmark and died; the account of the shooting itself comes only from the arresting side.

accounts.label: Denmark dispatch (arresting side)
accounts.gist: Davis came to the plantation residence for a settlement, saw the magistrate, ran for the woods and was shot in the back; he was pursued, captured and found wounded through the left shoulder and lungs.

accounts.label: Orangeburg dispatch and inquest
accounts.gist: Davis was captured by Magistrate Ray's constable and a posse, brought to the Orangeburg jail by the sheriff and died there; the physician found two gunshot wounds, in the stomach and left breast, and identification of the body was at first uncertain.

accounts.label: Bamberg Herald local item
accounts.gist: Magistrate Ray shot the man while making the arrest because he would not surrender; he died in the Orangeburg jail.

framing.detail: The Orangeburg Times and Democrat headlined 'MORTALLY WOUNDED' and closed that Davis killed the woman 'for no cause whatever' and 'met his just death' (A5).
The Bamberg Herald's version of the dispatch said the capture would have 'a wholesome effect upon the dark corners', and its local column praised Ray: 'Pity we did not have more officers like him.'
The Sumter Watchman and Southron ran the dispatch under 'NEGRO FUGITIVE FATALLY SHOT' with no comment, calling Davis 'Hunted for Uxoricide'.
The Orangeburg inquest dispatch reported the testimony, the alias and the doubt over identification, and described the body as 'a typical African'.
